articles.title: Watch The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview with Actor and Author Joe Manganiello
articles.content: You probably know Joe Manganiello as the werewolf Alcide Herveaux from True Blood or as the formidable villain Deathstroke from the DC universe, to name a few. With a career spanning everything from box-office hits like Magic Mike to binge-worthy TV shows and fantasy films, Manganiello has made a name for himself playing larger-than-life characters, but his personal story is even more powerful. This month, Manganiello released Bloodlines, a memoir about his seven-year battle with a mysterious illness that left him fighting for his life. “It’s a story about survival,” he tells us, describing the book as “a Trojan horse for a spiritual odyssey.” In it, the actor opens up about years of debilitating pain, uncertainty and a medical journey that, at one point, left him unable to walk and required the amputation of his large intestine. But Bloodlines is more than a story of illness. It’s a deeply personal look at transformation and what it means to find your way through the unimaginable. For this episode of The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview, we caught up with Manganiello to talk about Bloodlines, his journey from actor to author, and more. He gave us a peek into his writing process, revealed his favorite authors and made a case for the literary genre he thinks deserves a little more love. We also got the scoop on his go-to writing snack and the one character he’s played who holds a special place in his heart. Read on for our exclusive interview with Joe Manganiello, and shop his recommended reads below. (Bonus: We’ve included a few extra books that he talked about off camera too!) At Reader’s Digest, we’ve been sharing our favorite books for over 100 years. We’ve worked with bestselling authors including Susan Orlean, Janet Evanovich and Alex Haley, whose Pulitzer Prize–winning Roots grew out of a project funded by and originally published in the magazine. Through Fiction Favorites (formerly Select Editions and Condensed Books), Reader’s Digest has been publishing anthologies of abridged novels for decades. We’ve worked with some of the biggest names in fiction, including James Patterson, Ruth Ware, Kristin Hannah and more. The Reader’s Digest Book Club, helmed by Books Editor Tracey Neithercott, introduces readers to even more of today’s best fiction by upcoming, bestselling and award-winning authors. For this piece, Leigh Belz Ray interviewed actor and author Joe Manganiello. articles.title: Why Is Everyone Suddenly Talking About Stocking Up on Supplies for 90 Days—And Should You Be Worried?
articles.content:
Scroll through your social media feed right now, and you might be alarmed by the state of the world. Wars are raging, the midterms are upon us and tragic images of earthquakes and avalanches are filling our feeds. Is it any wonder everyone is talking about “prepping” all of a sudden?
Prepping, which is short for preparedness, just means keeping food and supplies on hand in case of emergencies. And it’s always been around. In fact, you could say that anyone who cans food or stores garden veggies in the cellar for the winter is a prepper. In many ways, planning for the future is part of our DNA.
But recently, you may have heard that the United States government issued a new advisory to stockpile 90 days’ worth of food and other supplies. Should we all be worried that something big is on the horizon? What’s behind all this talk? Ahead, I’ll break down what’s really going on and what you should do in response. Read on to learn the latest.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
First, let’s clear up a misconception: The 90-day timeline comes from the Pentagon’s new push to make U.S. military bases self-sustaining without outside intervention in the case of a war. But for regular people, the suggestion is much less onerous. In fact, it’s more in line with what you would do for a natural disaster, and in the U.S., the guidance hasn’t changed at all.
Over the past few weeks, several countries, including Britain, Japan and Germany, have issued new or revamped guidance to make sure residents stock enough food, water and other supplies to last anywhere from three days to more than a week. Here is a snapshot of what governments around the world are advising their citizens to do:
Climate change and natural disasters are big drivers of the push to get people prepared. Other reasons include cyberattacks, due to our heavy reliance on technology, and the rise of hostile foreign actors around the world. Here’s why being prepared is increasingly important today:
Climate change is accelerating the intensity and frequency of weather-related natural disasters, including heat waves, droughts and hurricanes. You don’t want to be caught off guard if help is days away. And with this year’s super El Niño, which could bring heavy rain and flooding to more than 40 states across the U.S., 2027 is shaping up to be a big one for weather disasters.
There’s also the issue of rising instability and migration due to climate change: According to the United Nations, climate disasters displaced nearly 46 million people in 2024. Having a few days’ worth of food and water on hand when the power goes out (or worse) could give you a lifeline when things look bleak.
Just last month, the world was on high alert due to a vulnerability in a programming language, PHP, used by 70% of the world’s websites. Before patches became available, millions of sites were attacked and multiple governments went offline as a precaution. What if your city’s electrical grid or water supply were affected?
And don’t discount the idea of hackers taking advantage of a natural disaster, says Lynn Budd, a former president of the National Emergency Management Association. “Everybody’s paying attention to the tornado, so our adversaries take advantage of that time and decide, ‘Oh, they’re busy with something else. Now’s the time to do a cyberattack or other types of attacks that may affect the critical infrastructure of a community,'” she told the Guardian.
War and instability are on the rise around the world, with conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East just two of the most visible. China, Iran, North Korea and Russia are cited as particular threats. The recent crisis over Starlink and Starshield satellite systems being suddenly unavailable to Ukrainians on the battlefield demonstrates that we are all vulnerable to actions beyond our control.
Sweden and Britain specifically noted hostile foreign actors as reasons for revamping their emergency guidance, and we should also note that being isolated by two major oceans, like we are here in the U.S., doesn’t provide as much of a buffer as it once did. Terror attacks and cyber threats can happen anywhere.
It depends on your perspective. Natural disasters and weather-related crises are definitely on the rise, so being prepared to hunker down at home for a few days after an emergency (or flee before one, if authorities advise that route) is just good planning. And keeping your cybersecurity defenses up is always smart given today’s threat environment.
But if you are hearing lots of panic about a new 90-day guidance from the government, remember that this applies to military bases, not the public. If anyone on your social media feed is encouraging you to prep an underground bunker with food and supplies for a coming three-month emergency, be circumspect, especially if they are selling something.
No. The U.S. government’s official advice remains the same: Three days’ worth of supplies is sufficient. Other countries also give recommendations of days, not months. Plus, groceries are expensive right now! Unless you have the space and money to bulk-buy food and water, do what makes you most comfortable.
Whether you prep for three days or 90, these are the things you should keep in your emergency preparedness kit:
You can find other ideas for your personal prepper kit at Ready.gov/kit.

  • Norway: The country’s DSB, or emergency preparedness agency, recommends Norwegians be prepared to live without help for one week.
  • Germany: The German government takes these tips even further, advising that residents have 10 days’ worth of supplies on hand in case of emergencies. If that’s not possible, three days is the bare minimum.

War and instability are on the rise around the world, with conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East just two of the most visible. China, Iran, North Korea and Russia are cited as particular threats. And keeping your cybersecurity defenses up is always smart given today’s threat environment.

But if you are hearing lots of panic about a new 90-day guidance from the government, remember that this applies to military bases, not the public. What kinds of supplies should you always have on hand?

Whether you prep for three days or 90, these are the things you should keep in your emergency preparedness kit:

  • Water: 1 gallon per person, per day
  • Nonperishable food: three days’ worth of food that never expires
  • First aid kit
  • Flashlight and extra batteries
  • Dust masks or respirators
  • Phone chargers and backup batteries
  • Weather radio
  • Manual can opener and basic tools
  • Personal sanitation: trash bags, twist ties and moist towelettes
  • Medication

You can find other ideas for your personal prepper kit at Ready.gov/kit.

articles.title: If Your Computer Is Acting Sluggish, This Secret Menu Could Have the Answers
articles.content:
There’s nothing more frustrating than a slow, sluggish computer. You know what I’m talking about: the lags, the cursor that refuses to cooperate, the loud fan whirring as you wait for it to boot up or open programs. All you want to do is check your email, play a game or finish up a work project, and suddenly your once-speedy computer thinks it’s 1999 again.
I’m a big believer in the restart. Taking a cue from the call-center employee whose first suggestion to any technical problem is to “unplug it and plug it back in,” I always restart my computer when it’s slow, and this does occasionally work. But other than that, I’m usually flying blind. I’m not the most technical person in the world, so what else can I do?
Well, there is something, and it’s right on my computer—and yours. While it won’t magically fix a lagging laptop (or desktop either), this secret menu can help diagnose problems and arm you with valuable information you can use to take further steps. And luckily, it doesn’t take a tech genius to take a peek under the hood, so to speak. Read on to learn all the insider intel.

On Windows PCs, it’s the Performance tab within your computer’s Task Manager app. On Macs, it’s called the Activity Monitor. Both apps track computer operations that are running in the background, as well as storage capacity and other key performance issues. They’re filled with valuable information that can help you figure out why your tech is bogging down for no apparent reason.
Both the Windows Performance tab and the Mac Activity Monitor capture tons of processes, but the five main ones that are helpful for diagnosing a slow computer are:
It’s easy, but there are few ways to get there, depending on your operating system.
There’s a lot of information in the Performance tab and Activity Monitor, and some of the more technical fixes are beyond the scope of this article. But you can start with some basic troubleshooting. When your computer is running slowly, open the Task Manager or Activity Monitor and be ready to jot down what you see.
Here are some top line things to look for and correct or research further.
Temporary spikes are not necessarily concerning, but if your CPU is consistently running near the maximum, the fan is loud or your computer is just plain slow, click over to the Processes tab on a PC (right above the Performance tab) or click the CPU column on a Mac. Close any resource-heavy apps that you’re not using, then restart and recheck.
Update or reinstall apps that continually use too many resources, and disable apps that start up automatically so they’re not constantly running in the background. You can also try cleaning your computer’s fan and vents with compressed air.
Heavy RAM usage often indicates too many things are running at once. Close apps you’re not using as well as browsers and/or excessive tabs that are open. Today’s browsers are much bigger resource hogs than they used to be, constantly loading and running videos, background scripts and ads. Restart. If the problem persists, consider adding more RAM.
If disk space is low, get rid of files, videos and images you no longer need. Close apps you’re not using, clear up space by running your computer’s disk cleanup function, and consider upgrading to a solid state drive instead of an older hard drive.
If your Activity Monitor or Performance tab shows high graphics-card usage, close video games and graphics-heavy apps and browsers. Restart your computer. If you continue to see that the GPU usage is high, you may need to update your graphics card.
If you’re having network connectivity problems, it’s always worth it to stop any downloads or heavy streaming activities that could be hung up. Restart your computer, make sure your router and/or modem are online, and run a speed test from your internet provider.
It’s worth trying some general fixes. Here are more tips that can help speed up your PC or Mac.

All you want to do is check your email, play a game or finish up a work project, and suddenly your once-speedy computer thinks it’s 1999 again.

I’m a big believer in the restart. Taking a cue from the call-center employee whose first suggestion to any technical problem is to “unplug it and plug it back in,” I always restart my computer when it’s slow, and this does occasionally work. But other than that, I’m usually flying blind. I’m not the most technical person in the world, so what else can I do?

Well, there is something, and it’s right on my computer—and yours. While it won’t magically fix a lagging laptop (or desktop either), this secret menu can help diagnose problems and arm you with valuable information you can use to take further steps. And luckily, it doesn’t take a tech genius to take a peek under the hood, so to speak. Read on to learn all the insider intel.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more tech, news, humor, cleaning, travel and fun facts all week long.

What is the secret menu that can diagnose a slow computer?

On Windows PCs, it’s the Performance tab within your computer’s Task Manager app. On Macs, it’s called the Activity Monitor. Both apps track computer operations that are running in the background, as well as storage capacity and other key performance issues. They’re filled with valuable information that can help you figure out why your tech is bogging down for no apparent reason.

What, exactly, do they tell you?

Both the Windows Performance tab and the Mac Activity Monitor capture tons of processes, but the five main ones that are helpful for diagnosing a slow computer are:

  • CPU usage: Your computer’s Central Processing Unit runs applications and software, performs calculations and generally acts as the “brain” of your computer. High CPU usage isn’t always bad, but if it’s high during certain operations, it could be a clue as to why your computer is dragging.
  • Memory (RAM): Random-access memory is your computer’s short-term memory. When you open an app, stream a movie or play a game, RAM is where your computer stores the data and files that the CPU needs right away while the application is in use.
  • Disk space: Your disk drive or hard drive is your computer’s long-term memory, where files, photos and other things that are not needed while applications are running are stored. But it can also store shorter-term files, especially if the RAM is inadequate.
  • Network processes: This information doesn’t pertain to your physical computer, per se, but a slow network connection can definitely be a reason it isn’t working as fast as it should on processes that require the internet.
  • GPU usage: This is your graphics processing unit, aka graphics card. It’s what’s needed to quickly render videos, movies, games and other graphics-heavy applications, as well as process your computer’s overall visuals.

How do you find these menus?

It’s easy, but there are few ways to get there, depending on your operating system.

Open the Performance tab on Windows computers

  • Use the Start button: Right-click on the Start button, select Task Manager and then navigate to the Performance tab on the left (it looks like a line graph).
  • Use the taskbar: Right-click on an empty part of the taskbar, select Task Manager and navigate to the Performance tab.
  • Use keyboard shortcuts: Hit Cntl + Shift + Esc at the same time to bring up the Task Manager directly. Alternatively, you can use Cntl + Alt + Del, and then select Task Manager from the menu.

Open the Activity Monitor on a Mac

  • Use Spotlight search: Hit the Command button and the space bar, then type in Activity Monitor and hit return. You can also find Spotlight by clicking the magnifying glass in the top right corner of your screen.
  • Use Finder: Open Finder on your dock, then go to the toolbar across the top and select Go > Utilities > Activity Monitor. If Finder is not in your dock, click any empty space on your desktop and the Finder toolbar will appear.
  • Use the Apps icon: Select the Apps icon from your dock, then type in Activity Monitor and hit return. Apps is a dedicated apps launcher within Spotlight that rolled out with the Tahoe update, but if you are running an older version you’ll know it as Launchpad.
  • Use a keyboard shortcut: Hit Fn + Shift + A to bring up the Apps search directly.

What are you looking for?

There’s a lot of information in the Performance tab and Activity Monitor, and some of the more technical fixes are beyond the scope of this article. But you can start with some basic troubleshooting. When your computer is running slowly, open the Task Manager or Activity Monitor and be ready to jot down what you see.

Here are some top line things to look for and correct or research further.

High CPU usage

Temporary spikes are not necessarily concerning, but if your CPU is consistently running near the maximum, the fan is loud or your computer is just plain slow, click over to the Processes tab on a PC (right above the Performance tab) or click the CPU column on a Mac. Close any resource-heavy apps that you’re not using, then restart and recheck.

Update or reinstall apps that continually use too many resources, and disable apps that start up automatically so they’re not constantly running in the background. You can also try cleaning your computer’s fan and vents with compressed air.

Low disk space and RAM

Heavy RAM usage often indicates too many things are running at once. Close apps you’re not using as well as browsers and/or excessive tabs that are open. Today’s browsers are much bigger resource hogs than they used to be, constantly loading and running videos, background scripts and ads. Restart. If the problem persists, consider adding more RAM.

If disk space is low, get rid of files, videos and images you no longer need. Close apps you’re not using, clear up space by running your computer’s disk cleanup function, and consider upgrading to a solid state drive instead of an older hard drive.

High GPU usage

If your Activity Monitor or Performance tab shows high graphics-card usage, close video games and graphics-heavy apps and browsers. Restart your computer. If you continue to see that the GPU usage is high, you may need to update your graphics card.

Network problems

If you’re having network connectivity problems, it’s always worth it to stop any downloads or heavy streaming activities that could be hung up. Restart your computer, make sure your router and/or modem are online, and run a speed test from your internet provider.

What else can you do to fix a slow computer?

It’s worth trying some general fixes. Here are more tips that can help speed up your PC or Mac.

  • Restart your computer. Yes, it sounds basic, but restarting does give your computer a little refresh by clearing out temporary files and closing background processes that might be hung up.
  • Close any programs you’re not using. Close extra tabs, browsers and apps. Change your startup settings so you don’t have a lot of programs running in the background that you’re not using.
  • Scan for malware. Viruses and malware can cause slowdowns, so run an antivirus program like Microsoft Defender Antivirus. For a Mac, Apple’s protection is built in and runs automatically.
  • Keep your computer updated. When your computer says you have software or operating-system updates available, download them. Recommended patches and anti-virus updates not only keep you safe from hackers—they can speed up a slow computer too.

articles.title: Need to Calm Down ASAP? Here’s How to Activate Your Vagus Nerve in 3 Minutes or Less and Keep Stress at Bay
articles.content:
I can usually tell when my anxiety has crossed from “I’m worried about this” into “I can’t seem to let this go” because the logic stops logic’ing. I might know, rationally, that whatever I’m spiraling about probably isn’t as catastrophic as it feels, but I still end up fixating on it until I’m dizzy and hyperaware of every thump in my chest.
That disconnect is frustrating … but it’s also potentially useful. The thing is, anxiety isn’t just spinning thoughts or sweaty palms; it’s happening in both your mind and your body at once. And that means you may be able to work on the physical side of the response instead of simply waiting for your brain to magically become reasonable.
The vagus nerve is one of the key players in that mind-body connection, helping your brain communicate with organs throughout your body and playing an important role in shifting you out of a stress response. If anxiety can send that whole system in one panicked direction, there’s a lot of interest in whether you can work from the body up to help steer it back toward calmer waters, and there’s some pretty convincing science behind it.
To learn how to stimulate the vagus nerve, I spoke with Richard Gevirtz, PhD, a psychology professor at the California School of Professional Psychology at Alliant University, and Christopher Austelle, MD, a board-certified psychiatrist and a clinical assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University. Read on to learn how to work with your nervous system to calm down a whole lot faster.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more wellness, science, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
The vagus nerve is one of the body’s major communication routes. Though we colloquially refer to it in the singular, we actually have two vagal nerves. They travel from the brainstem through either side of the neck and then into the chest and abdomen, passing the heart, lungs and digestive tract along the way.
Comprised of more than 200,000 nerve fibers, the vagus nerve is also the primary nerve involved in the parasympathetic nervous system, explains Gevirtz. Quick biology refresh: Your sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems help manage many of the things your body does automatically. The sympathetic side helps mobilize you when something requires action, while the parasympathetic side helps bring things back toward rest and recovery afterward. The vagus nerve can help calm some of the physical changes that happen when you’re anxious. As a major pathway of the parasympathetic nervous system, it helps regulate heart rate, breathing and digestion, as well as helps your body return toward rest after a stress response.
During stress, Gevirtz explains, sympathetic activity normally increases while parasympathetic activity temporarily drops, a process sometimes called vagal withdrawal. That shift helps your body gear up to respond; once the demand has passed, the balance should move back toward rest and recovery. You can see part of that process with every breath. Your heart rate naturally rises slightly as you inhale and falls as you exhale, a pattern the vagus nerve helps regulate. Those beat-to-beat differences contribute to heart rate variability, or HRV.
A 2022 meta-analysis published in Psychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences found that people with anxiety disorders tended to have lower parasympathetic activity at rest. In other words, the part of the nervous system that helps you wind down may be less active in people with anxiety. But that doesn’t necessarily mean the vagus nerve itself isn’t working properly.
For the most part, it does. Your vagus nerve isn’t a muscle that becomes weak because you forgot to exercise it, and it generally doesn’t need to be “reset.”

“One of the techniques with the most evidence and the most convincing evidence is slow breathing,” Dr. Austelle says. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis published in Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews looked at more than 200 studies and found that slow breathing increased signs of parasympathetic activity—the “rest, digest and restore” side of the nervous system—both while people were breathing slowly and afterward. Gevirtz generally recommends slowing to about four to seven breaths per minute. That works out to one full inhale-and-exhale cycle roughly every nine to 15 seconds—not holding your breath, just breathing more slowly and continuously. “It has to be effortless breathing,” he says.
Dr. Austelle says the exhale may be particularly important. To try it, sit comfortably, gradually slow your breathing and let your exhale last a little longer than your inhale. Don’t force enormous breaths; if you feel lightheaded, return to your normal breathing.
Cyclic sighing gives you a more specific pattern to follow. Inhale slowly through your nose, take a second, smaller inhale to fill your lungs a little more, and then slowly and fully exhale through your mouth. There isn’t a specific number of seconds you need to hit; the emphasis is on that double inhale followed by a longer exhale.
A 2023 study published in Cell Reports Medicine had adults practice cyclic sighing, two other breathing exercises or mindfulness meditation for five minutes a day over about a month. Actual VNS is different: These devices stimulate the nerve directly with electricity. According to the National Institute of Mental Health, implanted VNS is used for certain medical conditions, including treatment-resistant epilepsy and depression. Noninvasive, or transcutaneous, VNS delivers electrical stimulation through the skin and is being studied for a range of psychiatric and neurological conditions.
For everyday stress management, though, Gevirtz says evidence for commercial noninvasive devices remains mixed, particularly when researchers compare them with sham devices that feel similar but don’t provide the same stimulation.

These techniques can be useful when anxiety is making your whole system feel revved up, but they can’t address every reason you might be anxious. If you’re anxious most of the time, having panic attacks, losing sleep over it or starting to avoid parts of your life because of it, that’s worth bringing to a health-care or mental-health professional.
And sometimes the problem really is the problem. Breathing more slowly may help you feel steadier before a difficult conversation, but it won’t make the conversation disappear. It can, however, make it easier to walk into that conversation without feeling like your body has decided it’s an emergency.
That’s really the point for me. I’m not trying to breathe my way out of having problems. But it’s powerful to know I can use something as simple as my breathing to actually turn down the volume on anxiety when it starts taking over.

articles.title: Here’s How “Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon” Originated—And Why You Might Actually Be Six Degrees Away from Him Too
articles.content:
We’ve all had those it’s-a-small-world moments when we discover we’re randomly connected to someone else. It happened to me recently while traveling in Athens, Greece, where I struck up a new friendship with a fellow traveler from Italy. We quickly discovered, to our surprise, that we had a mutual friend.
You’ve most likely heard of the theory six degrees of separation, which suggests that everyone on Earth is connected through a chain of no more than six people. Theoretically, that means you could trace your connection to just about anyone, whether it’s a person you just met in a foreign country, like I did, or a famous Hollywood star.
Of course, this concept is best illustrated with one particular Hollywood star, in the popular parlor game Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon, where players attempt to connect any actor to Kevin Bacon through the films on their résumé. For example, Christian Slater is just one degree away, having starred alongside Bacon in 1995’s Murder in the First. The late James Dean, meanwhile, is an iconic actor from generations ago, but he’s still just three degrees away—Dean appeared with Dennis Hopper in 1955’s Rebel Without a Cause, Hopper starred with Chris Penn in the 1993 movie True Romance, and Penn and Bacon were both in the ’80s classic Footloose.
Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon demonstrates how surprisingly short the paths between people can be. Still, there are some questions to consider. As a former celebrity journalist, for example, I once interviewed Bacon at a party. Does that count as a connection to him since it was so fleeting? And does the theory translate to everyday people around the globe, both with and without Kevin Bacon in the mix?
To get to the bottom of this, I spoke with Albert-László Barabási, PhD, who teaches at Northeastern University and Harvard Medical School and researches complex networks, and Jure Leskovec, PhD, a computer science professor at Stanford University. Read on to learn how the game got its start, plus whether the underlying concept behind Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon actually holds up to scientific scrutiny—and what it could mean for you.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Three friends—Brian Turtle, Mike Ginelli and Craig Fass—came up with the concept as a college drinking game when they were students at Albright College in Pennsylvania more than 30 years ago. “We were just a couple of college guys who watched movies like JFK and Footloose, and found that in 1994, Kevin Bacon was everywhere,” Turtle said on the People of Play online gaming community of the pastime that “took on a life of its own.”
The Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon game, he joked, “was kind of a ‘stupid human trick,’” but it was one that got the college pals interviewed by everyone from Jon Stewart to Howard Stern. In 1996, the trio even created a board game, produced by the newly formed company Endless Games, where Turtle has worked ever since. “After graduation in ’95, I never thought I’d hear about [Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon] again, but it never went away!” he said.
Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon became popular in the 1990s, but the idea behind it is based on real research and theories that go back much further. In the 1960s, Yale psychologist Stanley Milgram conducted a “small world” experiment to explore how closely people were linked via their social networks. He asked participants to attempt to get letters to a specific person by forwarding them to acquaintances they believed might help get the letters closer to their destination. (More on how that experiment went in a minute.)
The idea that actors can be linked to Kevin Bacon—or that two seemingly random people can be connected—through a short chain of acquaintances does indeed hold up. And those ties may be much smaller than six degrees, according to research. Here’s how it shakes out.
You’d be hard-pressed not to find a connection between Bacon and nearly any other working actor. Because actors often appear in multiple films with different co-stars, their projects create a sprawling web of work that can be used to trace a path to Bacon.
Don’t believe it? The website Oracle of Bacon lets you enter an actor’s name and see how they’re connected to him, step by step. Even some pretty obscure actors in the database can be linked to Bacon through his network. Ever heard of the Croatian actor Rade Šerbedźija? Maybe not, but he’s just one degree from Bacon, thanks to the film X-Men: First Class.
The broader six degrees of separation theory can be applied to link anyone to Bacon. Yes, anyone—including you! Barabási, who’s a pioneer in network science, says we may be connected to almost anyone in the world not by six degrees, but by as few as three to four steps, even if only through a chain of acquaintances.
“A typical person knows about 1,000 people on a first-name basis, so there are roughly—and this is a simplification, but it works—1,000 × 1,000 people two handshakes away and 10^9 people (10 to the ninth power, or 1 followed by nine zeros) three handshakes away,” he says. For those who aren’t so mathematically inclined, that’s 1 million people two steps away, and 1 billion people three steps away, and each additional step expands that network exponentially. “That is the secret of six degrees.”
But throw in social media, and the definition of a connection makes the picture a little more complicated. According to Nature Reviews Physics, Milgram’s letter chains typically ranged from two to 10 links, but today’s technology and online social networks have reduced those connection numbers massively. Just think of all the people you’re technically “friends” with on Facebook or connected to on LinkedIn—and how many of those same people you wouldn’t recognize by name.
Leskovec, whose research spans network science, AI and machine learning, examined Microsoft’s instant-messaging network and found two people were separated by an average of 6.6 steps in the network of approximately 240 million people. “It does not mean everyone was directly connected,” he explains. “Rather, local circles overlap enough that only a handful of steps usually link people across the network.”
In 2016, Facebook revealed that the average separation between two users on its platform had shrunk to 3.57 degrees, down from 3.74 in 2011. That’s an incredibly small number on a network that spans billions of people, and it’s likely getting smaller. Still, a short chain of online connections doesn’t equate to really knowing someone.
So six degrees of separation isn’t a hard-and-fast rule, but the separation between people is shockingly small. “‘Six degrees’ is best understood as a memorable approximation of typical connectivity, not a universal upper bound,” Leskovec says.
Turtle, the man who co-created Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon, says that the actor wasn’t thrilled with the game at first because “he thought we were making fun of him.”
That began to change in 1995, when Turtle and his friends were on The Jon Stewart Show to demonstrate their uncanny knack for tracing any Hollywood actor back to Bacon, who was also a guest on the program that night. “Somebody with a bigger ego might have told us to go pound sand, but Kevin warmed up to the game and even wound up writing a rather hilarious prologue to that bestselling paperback [on the topic],” Turtle wrote on People of Play.
Once Bacon realized the game was all in good fun, he embraced it and took the idea a step further by founding SixDegrees.org—a nonprofit foundation that uses storytelling and community-first campaigns to bring people together and fight disconnection in society.
Well, you probably shouldn’t call up Kevin Bacon and tell him you know him through a friend. But by all means, continue playing the game! It’s neat to think about the larger idea of discovering connections between people, whether it’s linking actors to Kevin Bacon or finding ties within our own social circles.
The concept also offers a great reminder that we’re all more connected than it may first appear. Through family relationships, friendships and even chance encounters, our seemingly separate worlds often overlap in surprising ways. As Bacon notes in a video for SixDegrees.org, it’s all about “thinking about the connections that we all have.”
And it’s important to keep in mind that those connections affect society, for better or worse. As Leskovec notes, “it matters because information, opportunities, behaviors (and sometimes misinformation or disease) can spread across a large population very quickly.” In other words, the world is small and our influence is outsized, so go forth and do good.

We’ve all had those it’s-a-small-world moments when we discover we’re randomly connected to someone else. It happened to me recently while traveling in Athens, Greece, where I struck up a new friendship with a fellow traveler from Italy. We quickly discovered, to our surprise, that we had a mutual friend.

You’ve most likely heard of the theory six degrees of separation, which suggests that everyone on Earth is connected through a chain of no more than six people. Theoretically, that means you could trace your connection to just about anyone, whether it’s a person you just met in a foreign country, like I did, or a famous Hollywood star.

Of course, this concept is best illustrated with one particular Hollywood star, in the popular parlor game Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon, where players attempt to connect any actor to Kevin Bacon through the films on their résumé. For example, Christian Slater is just one degree away, having starred alongside Bacon in 1995’s Murder in the First. The late James Dean, meanwhile, is an iconic actor from generations ago, but he’s still just three degrees away—Dean appeared with Dennis Hopper in 1955’s Rebel Without a Cause, Hopper starred with Chris Penn in the 1993 movie True Romance, and Penn and Bacon were both in the ’80s classic Footloose.

Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon demonstrates how surprisingly short the paths between people can be. Still, there are some questions to consider. As a former celebrity journalist, for example, I once interviewed Bacon at a party. Does that count as a connection to him since it was so fleeting? And does the theory translate to everyday people around the globe, both with and without Kevin Bacon in the mix?

To get to the bottom of this, I spoke with Albert-László Barabási, PhD, who teaches at Northeastern University and Harvard Medical School and researches complex networks, and Jure Leskovec, PhD, a computer science professor at Stanford University. Read on to learn how the game got its start, plus whether the underlying concept behind Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon actually holds up to scientific scrutiny—and what it could mean for you.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

What’s the origin story behind Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon?

Three friends—Brian Turtle, Mike Ginelli and Craig Fass—came up with the concept as a college drinking game when they were students at Albright College in Pennsylvania more than 30 years ago. “We were just a couple of college guys who watched movies like JFK and Footloose, and found that in 1994, Kevin Bacon was everywhere,” Turtle said on the People of Play online gaming community of the pastime that “took on a life of its own.”

The Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon game, he joked, “was kind of a ‘stupid human trick,’” but it was one that got the college pals interviewed by everyone from Jon Stewart to Howard Stern. In 1996, the trio even created a board game, produced by the newly formed company Endless Games, where Turtle has worked ever since. “After graduation in ’95, I never thought I’d hear about [Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon] again, but it never went away!” he said.

Was this a brand-new concept?

Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon became popular in the 1990s, but the idea behind it is based on real research and theories that go back much further. In the 1960s, Yale psychologist Stanley Milgram conducted a “small world” experiment to explore how closely people were linked via their social networks. He asked participants to attempt to get letters to a specific person by forwarding them to acquaintances they believed might help get the letters closer to their destination. (More on how that experiment went in a minute.)

Does this theory actually hold up in the world at large?

The idea that actors can be linked to Kevin Bacon—or that two seemingly random people can be connected—through a short chain of acquaintances does indeed hold up. And those ties may be much smaller than six degrees, according to research. Here’s how it shakes out.

Six degrees of Kevin Bacon

You’d be hard-pressed not to find a connection between Bacon and nearly any other working actor. Because actors often appear in multiple films with different co-stars, their projects create a sprawling web of work that can be used to trace a path to Bacon.

Don’t believe it? The website Oracle of Bacon lets you enter an actor’s name and see how they’re connected to him, step by step. Even some pretty obscure actors in the database can be linked to Bacon through his network. Ever heard of the Croatian actor Rade Šerbedźija? Maybe not, but he’s just one degree from Bacon, thanks to the film X-Men: First Class.

Six degrees of anyone and everyone

The broader six degrees of separation theory can be applied to link anyone to Bacon. Yes, anyone—including you! Barabási, who’s a pioneer in network science, says we may be connected to almost anyone in the world not by six degrees, but by as few as three to four steps, even if only through a chain of acquaintances.

“A typical person knows about 1,000 people on a first-name basis, so there are roughly—and this is a simplification, but it works—1,000 × 1,000 people two handshakes away and 10^9 people (10 to the ninth power, or 1 followed by nine zeros) three handshakes away,” he says. For those who aren’t so mathematically inclined, that’s 1 million people two steps away, and 1 billion people three steps away, and each additional step expands that network exponentially. “That is the secret of six degrees.”

But throw in social media, and the definition of a connection makes the picture a little more complicated. According to Nature Reviews Physics, Milgram’s letter chains typically ranged from two to 10 links, but today’s technology and online social networks have reduced those connection numbers massively. Just think of all the people you’re technically “friends” with on Facebook or connected to on LinkedIn—and how many of those same people you wouldn’t recognize by name.

Leskovec, whose research spans network science, AI and machine learning, examined Microsoft’s instant-messaging network and found two people were separated by an average of 6.6 steps in the network of approximately 240 million people. “It does not mean everyone was directly connected,” he explains. “Rather, local circles overlap enough that only a handful of steps usually link people across the network.”

In 2016, Facebook revealed that the average separation between two users on its platform had shrunk to 3.57 degrees, down from 3.74 in 2011. That’s an incredibly small number on a network that spans billions of people, and it’s likely getting smaller. Still, a short chain of online connections doesn’t equate to really knowing someone.

So six degrees of separation isn’t a hard-and-fast rule, but the separation between people is shockingly small. “‘Six degrees’ is best understood as a memorable approximation of typical connectivity, not a universal upper bound,” Leskovec says.

How does Kevin Bacon feel about all of this?

Turtle, the man who co-created Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon, says that the actor wasn’t thrilled with the game at first because “he thought we were making fun of him.”

That began to change in 1995, when Turtle and his friends were on The Jon Stewart Show to demonstrate their uncanny knack for tracing any Hollywood actor back to Bacon, who was also a guest on the program that night. “Somebody with a bigger ego might have told us to go pound sand, but Kevin warmed up to the game and even wound up writing a rather hilarious prologue to that bestselling paperback [on the topic],” Turtle wrote on People of Play.

Once Bacon realized the game was all in good fun, he embraced it and took the idea a step further by founding SixDegrees.org—a nonprofit foundation that uses storytelling and community-first campaigns to bring people together and fight disconnection in society.

What should you do with this idea?

Well, you probably shouldn’t call up Kevin Bacon and tell him you know him through a friend. But by all means, continue playing the game! It’s neat to think about the larger idea of discovering connections between people, whether it’s linking actors to Kevin Bacon or finding ties within our own social circles.

The concept also offers a great reminder that we’re all more connected than it may first appear. Through family relationships, friendships and even chance encounters, our seemingly separate worlds often overlap in surprising ways. As Bacon notes in a video for SixDegrees.org, it’s all about “thinking about the connections that we all have.”

And it’s important to keep in mind that those connections affect society, for better or worse. As Leskovec notes, “it matters because information, opportunities, behaviors (and sometimes misinformation or disease) can spread across a large population very quickly.” In other words, the world is small and our influence is outsized, so go forth and do good.

About the experts

  • Albert-László Barabási, PhD, is a distinguished professor at Northeastern University and faculty at the Division of Network Medicine at Harvard Medical School. He is one of the founders of network medicine, and his current research uncovers how complex networks—from genes to diseases—shape health and human longevity.
  • Jure Leskovec, PhD, is a professor of computer science at Stanford University, where he is affiliated with the Stanford AI Lab, the Machine Learning Group and the Center for Research on Foundation Models. His research spans network science, AI and machine learning, as well as computational biomedicine.
